# ghax

A minimalist, terminal-native agent written in Go that takes on a **shape** — a design partner,
a spec implementer, a telemetry watcher — and runs as a well-behaved citizen of the
[herdr](https://herdr.dev/) runtime.

Disclaimer: This works for me -- that's the entire guarantee. Built with AI in the loop, so check
your own biases before you love it or hate it on principle. Use at your own risk, fork freely, and
don't @ me when it explodes. (But do drop me a note if it helps -- pay it forward.)

> **Status: working, early.** The engine, three loop modes, provider adapters (local, OpenAI,
> Anthropic, and an offline mock), the compiled-in tools, config/shapes, sessions, and the herdr
> client are implemented and tested (`make test`). It has not yet been exercised against a wide
> range of live models. See [VISION.md](./VISION.md) for the why and [DESIGN.md](./DESIGN.md) for
> the how.
>
> Try it with no model backend at all: `make build && ./bin/ghax --provider mock -p "hello"`.

---

## The problem

You end up wanting the same agent for very different jobs. One moment it should be a thinking
partner reasoning through a design with a big model. The next it should grind a project to a
written spec, unattended. Sometimes it shouldn't be coding at all — it should sit on a telemetry
stream and react when something interesting happens.

Those jobs want different prompts, tools, models, and rhythms, but the machine underneath them is
the same: read input, build context, ask a model, run tools, loop. Most agents make you pick one
job and one runtime. And when you run several at once — across a laptop, a build server, and an
edge box — you lose track of which one is working, which is stuck, and which is done.

ghax is one small binary that solves both. You give it a **shape** (config, not code) and it
becomes the agent that job needs. And because it reports its real state to herdr, a fleet of
shaped instances stays legible: herdr never has to guess what any ghax is doing.

## Why build this?

Because the agent should run on **your** inference, not someone else's API.

The premise: you run one or more inference servers — Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp, TGI — on a
workstation, a GPU box, a DGX, or a small cluster, and you front them with
[LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/), which exposes a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint with model
routing, fallback, aliases, key management, and usage accounting. ghax points at that one
endpoint. That buys you:

- **Traffic stays on your network by default.** ghax only ever talks to your LiteLLM endpoint.
  Nothing leaves your network unless *you* wire an external backend into LiteLLM — and that is a
  single, deliberate config change in one file, not a decision scattered across every agent.
- **One place for config, keys, routing, and monitoring.** Point a whole fleet of ghax agents at a
  single LiteLLM: model choices, provider keys, routing and fallback, budgets, rate limits, and
  usage logging all live there. You configure and observe every agent from one control point.
- **No per-token cost and no rate limits** you did not set yourself — for anything served locally.
- **The same agent everywhere.** One static Go binary, from an edge SBC to a Kubernetes pod, all
  talking to the same gateway.

Most agents assume a hosted cloud API, a heavyweight runtime, or a plugin marketplace. ghax
assumes you own the inference and want a small, inspectable, scriptable tool that takes on whatever
shape the job needs — and stays legible when you run a fleet of them under herdr. It descends from
[hax](https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/hax) and keeps its restraint; [VISION.md](./VISION.md)
records the full rationale and the deliberate omissions.

## Why this and not hax, pi, or OMP?

These are the neighbors. Short version: **ghax is hax's philosophy in Go, with a first-class
observe mode and herdr citizenship, built to point at your own LiteLLM-fronted inference.**

**vs [hax](https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/hax)** — hax is the direct ancestor, and ghax
keeps almost all of it: one small binary, local-first, inspectable, no plugins / MCP / permission
prompts, presets. What ghax changes:

- **Go, not C.** One statically cross-compiled binary for the whole spectrum — edge SBC → server →
  Kubernetes pod — with goroutines and `context` instead of hand-rolled threads. Same footprint
  discipline, less ceremony.
- **A first-class observe loop.** hax is request/response only; it can't sit on a telemetry stream
  and react. ghax's `observe` mode (sources → triggers → bounded reactions) is a peer of the REPL.
- **herdr-native.** ghax ships authoritative status hooks, a screen manifest, and shape/model
  metadata so a fleet is legible; hax is just a well-behaved Unix tool.
- **Shapes select the loop mode**, not only the prompt/model — so one binary is a REPL, a script
  step, or a watcher.

If you only want coding at the terminal, in C, with no watcher and no fleet, use hax — it's the
smaller, more proven thing. ghax is for when you also want the observe mode, herdr fleet
visibility, and Go's one-binary reach across your hardware.

**vs pi and OMP (oh-my-pi)** — these are richer, batteries-included agents with **package
ecosystems** ([pi.dev](https://pi.dev/) packages) and full TUIs, and they're first-class herdr
citizens too. ghax goes the other way on purpose:

- **No package runtime, plugin ABI, or marketplace.** Extension is config, `SKILL.md`, and external
  CLIs — the hax stance. Less power, far less surface to audit, version, or break.
- **One small static binary, not a platform.** Nothing to install beyond the binary; nothing
  dynamic to load at runtime.
- **Shaped for non-coding jobs too.** The same engine watches telemetry or processes a stream, not
  only writes code.
- **Citizen, not conductor.** ghax reports state to herdr but does not orchestrate peers or host a
  plugin surface — orchestration stays outside the process.

If you want the ecosystem — installable packages, a plugin surface, a full-screen TUI — reach for
pi or OMP. ghax is for when you want the *smallest* thing that can be many shapes, runs on your own
inference, and stays legible in a fleet.

The common thread: **you own the inference (LiteLLM in front of your servers), you want one
auditable binary, and you want it to become whatever shape the job needs.**

## What it is

- **One static Go binary.** Cross-compiles for servers, SBCs, and edge devices. Small footprint —
  it leaves the RAM for your models.
- **Your inference, via LiteLLM.** Point ghax at a LiteLLM proxy fronting your inference server(s)
  (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp). One OpenAI-compatible endpoint, many models; `type: local`
  auto-discovers the served model. Cloud APIs work too, but self-hosted is the assumption. See
  [Model backend](#model-backend-litellm-in-front-of-your-inference).
- **Three loop modes.** `interactive` (a REPL), `oneshot` (`-p`, clean stdout, resumable — the
  Unix seam for scripts), and `observe` (a long-running, event-driven watcher).
- **A herdr citizen.** Reports authoritative status (`working`/`idle`/`done`) and rich
  metadata over the herdr socket, ships a screen manifest as a fallback, and resumes cleanly. It
  does not orchestrate other agents — that stays outside the process.

**ghax** is a minimalist, terminal-native AI agent written in Go, living at `/home/gherlein/h/src/er/agents/ghax`. Key points:

- **Concept**: One small static binary that takes on a **shape** (a config, not code) — e.g. a design partner, a spec implementer, a telemetry watcher — and becomes whatever agent the job needs.
- **Runtime citizen of herdr**: reports authoritative status (`working`/`idle`/`done`) and metadata to the [herdr](https://herdr.dev/) fleet-management runtime.
- **Three loop modes**: `interactive` (REPL), `oneshot` (`-p` flag, scriptable/Unix-friendly), and `observe` (long-running event-driven watcher on telemetry/streams).
- **Model backend philosophy**: designed to point at *your own* inference (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp, etc.) fronted by LiteLLM's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so traffic stays on your network. Cloud APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic) and an offline `mock` provider are also supported.
- **Minimalist by design**: no MCP, no plugin ABI/marketplace, no per-command permission prompts — deliberately restrained, following the philosophy of its ancestor [hax](https://github.com/OleksandrChekhovskyi/hax) (a C agent). Extension happens via external CLIs, skills, and config only.
- **Compared to pi/OMP**: those are richer, plugin/package-based ecosystems with full TUIs; ghax intentionally stays a small, auditable single binary instead.

Structure in the repo:
- `cmd/`, `internal/` — Go source (engine, provider adapters, config/shapes, sessions, herdr client, tools)
- `bin/` — build output
- `examples/` — example shapes/configs
- `DESIGN.md` — architecture/implementation details
- `VISION.md` — rationale and deliberate design omissions
- `NAMES.md`, `README.md`, `Makefile`, `LICENSE`

Status per README: "working, early" — core engine, loop modes, provider adapters, tools, config/shapes, sessions, and herdr client are implemented and tested (`make test`), but not yet broadly exercised against many live models.
